---
<!-- ex-1: body_md -->
Every automorphism of \(A_2\) has the form
		\[
		\rho(x_1)=\lambda_1x_1^ax_2^c,\qquad
		\rho(x_2)=\lambda_2x_1^bx_2^d,
		\]
		where \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\in\Bbbk^\ast\) and
		\[
		M_\rho=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix},
		\qquad ad-bc=\pm1.
		\]
<!-- end ex-1 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{th:LFD-Laurent}
		A derivation \(D\in\operatorname{Der}_{\Bbbk}(A_n)\) is locally finite
		if and only if
		\[
		D=D_\mu=\sum_{i=1}^n\mu_i E_i
		\]
		for some \(\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n)^T\in\Bbbk^n\).
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:isotropy-condition-A2}
		An automorphism
		\[
		\rho(x_1)=\lambda_1x_1^ax_2^c,\qquad
		\rho(x_2)=\lambda_2x_1^bx_2^d
		\]
		commutes with \(D_\mu\) if and only if
		\[
		(a-1)\mu_1+c\mu_2=0,\qquad
		b\mu_1+(d-1)\mu_2=0.
		\]
		Equivalently, \(\mu^TM_\rho=\mu^T\).
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
For the two generators, we have
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			\rho D_\mu(x_1)&=\mu_1\lambda_1x_1^ax_2^c,&
			D_\mu\rho(x_1)&=(a\mu_1+c\mu_2)\lambda_1x_1^ax_2^c,\\
			\rho D_\mu(x_2)&=\mu_2\lambda_2x_1^bx_2^d,&
			D_\mu\rho(x_2)&=(b\mu_1+d\mu_2)\lambda_2x_1^bx_2^d.
		\end{aligned}
		\]
		Equality on \(x_1,x_2\) gives exactly the stated conditions.
		It also implies equality on their inverses, by
		\(D(u^{-1})=-u^{-2}D(u)\), and then on all of \(A_2\) by the
		Leibniz rule and linearity. Finally,
		\[
		\mu^TM_\rho=(a\mu_1+c\mu_2,\ b\mu_1+d\mu_2),
		\]
		which gives the matrix formulation.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:independent-A2}
		If \(\mu_1,\mu_2\) are linearly independent over \(\mathbb Q\), then
		\(\operatorname{Aut}_{D_\mu}(A_2)\) consists precisely of the diagonal automorphisms
		\[
		\rho(x_1)=\lambda_1x_1,\qquad
		\rho(x_2)=\lambda_2x_2,
		\qquad \lambda_1,\lambda_2\in\Bbbk^\ast.
		\]
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The two relations in Proposition~\ref{prop:isotropy-condition-A2}
		force \(a=d=1\) and \(b=c=0\). Conversely, every diagonal
		automorphism commutes with \(D_\mu\).
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:dependent-A2}
		With the notation above, the automorphisms commuting with \(D_\mu\)
		are precisely
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			\rho(x_1)&=\lambda_1x_1^{1+qu}x_2^{-pu},\\
			\rho(x_2)&=\lambda_2x_1^{qv}x_2^{1-pv},
		\end{aligned}
		\qquad
		\begin{gathered}
			\lambda_1,\lambda_2\in\Bbbk^\ast,\\
			u,v\in\mathbb Z,\qquad qu-pv\in\{0,-2\}.
		\end{gathered}
		\]
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Write \(M_\rho=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\).
		By Proposition~\ref{prop:isotropy-condition-A2}, commutation is equivalent to
		\[
		p(a-1)+qc=0,\qquad pb+q(d-1)=0.
		\]
		Thus both columns of \(M_\rho-I_2\) belong to the kernel of
		\[
		\mathbb Z^2\longrightarrow\mathbb Z,
		\qquad (h,k)^T\longmapsto ph+qk.
		\]
		As \(\gcd(p,q)=1\), this kernel is generated by \((q,-p)^T\).
		Consequently, for some \(u,v\in\mathbb Z\),
		\[
		M_\rho-I_2=\begin{pmatrix}q\\-p\end{pmatrix}(u\ v),
		\qquad
		M_\rho=\begin{pmatrix}1+qu&qv\\-pu&1-pv\end{pmatrix}.
		\]
		Its determinant is \(1+qu-pv\). Therefore, this matrix is unimodular
		if and only if \(qu-pv\in\{0,-2\}\).
		Conversely, every matrix of this form with determinant \(\pm1\)
		fixes \((p,q)\) on the right and defines, for arbitrary nonzero
		\(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\), a commuting automorphism.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- rem-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:det-one-A2}
		The automorphisms in Proposition~\ref{prop:dependent-A2} whose
		exponent matrices have determinant one are obtained by taking
		\(u=pt\) and \(v=qt\), with \(t\in\mathbb Z\). Their exponent matrices are
		\[
		M_t=\begin{pmatrix}
			1+pqt&q^2t\\-p^2t&1-pqt
		\end{pmatrix}.
		\]
		This follows from \(qu-pv=0\) and \(\gcd(p,q)=1\).
<!-- end rem-1 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{th:isotropy-LFD-A2}
		Let \(D_\mu\ne0\) be a locally finite derivation of \(A_2\).
		If \(\mu_1,\mu_2\) are linearly independent over \(\mathbb Q\),
		its commuting automorphisms are exactly the diagonal scalings.
		Otherwise, they are precisely the automorphisms parametrized in
		Proposition~\ref{prop:dependent-A2}.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
\label{isotropy-condition-An}
		Let \(\rho\in\operatorname{Aut}_{\Bbbk}(A_n)\), with
		\(\rho(x_i)=\lambda_i x^{m_i}\) and
		\(M_\rho=(m_1\ \cdots\ m_n)\).
		Then
		\[
		\rho D_\mu=D_\mu\rho
		\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
		\mu^Tm_i=\mu_i\ \text{for every }i
		\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
		\mu^TM_\rho=\mu^T.
		\]
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
For each \(i\),
		\[
		\rho D_\mu(x_i)=\mu_i\lambda_i x^{m_i},
		\qquad D_\mu\rho(x_i)=(\mu^Tm_i)\lambda_i x^{m_i}.
		\]
		These expressions agree exactly when \(\mu^Tm_i=\mu_i\).
		As in the two-dimensional case, equality on the \(x_i\) implies
		equality on their inverses and hence on all of \(A_n\).
		The conditions on the columns are equivalent to the stated matrix equality.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:adapted-basis}
		There exists a basis
		\(u_1,\ldots,u_r,v_1,\ldots,v_s\) of \(\mathbb Z^n\), where
		\(s=n-r\), such that \(v_1,\ldots,v_s\) is a basis of \(L_\mu\).
		In particular, \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}L_\mu=n-r\).
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Consider
		\[
		\varphi_\mu:\mathbb Z^n\longrightarrow(\Bbbk,+),
		\qquad a\longmapsto\mu^Ta.
		\]
		Its kernel is \(L_\mu\), and its image is the finitely generated
		torsion-free abelian group \(\mathbb Z\mu_1+\cdots+\mathbb Z\mu_n\),
		which has rank \(r\). Choose a basis \(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_r\)
		of this image and lifts \(u_i\in\mathbb Z^n\) with
		\(\varphi_\mu(u_i)=\gamma_i\). As a subgroup of \(\mathbb Z^n\),
		\(L_\mu\) is free abelian; choose a basis \(v_1,\ldots,v_s\).
		For every \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), write
		\(\varphi_\mu(z)=\sum_i a_i\gamma_i\). Then
		\(z-\sum_i a_i u_i\in L_\mu\), so the \(u_i\) and \(v_j\)
		generate \(\mathbb Z^n\). If
		\(\sum_i a_i u_i+\sum_j b_jv_j=0\), applying \(\varphi_\mu\)
		first gives all \(a_i=0\), and then all \(b_j=0\).
		Thus these vectors form a basis, and \(r+s=n\).
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:structure-Gmu}
		Choose a basis as in Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted-basis}, and set
		\[
		U=(u_1\ \cdots\ u_r\ v_1\ \cdots\ v_s)\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb Z).
		\]
		Then an integer matrix \(M\) is unimodular and satisfies
		\(\mu^TM=\mu^T\) if and only if
		\[
		M=U\begin{pmatrix}I_r&0\\B&C\end{pmatrix}U^{-1},
		\qquad
		B\in M_{s\times r}(\mathbb Z),\quad C\in\operatorname{GL}_s(\mathbb Z).
		\]
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Put \(\gamma_i=\varphi_\mu(u_i)\). These elements form a basis of
		\(\operatorname{Im}\varphi_\mu\) and are therefore linearly independent over
		\(\mathbb Q\). Moreover,
		\[
		\mu^TU=(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_r,0,\ldots,0).
		\]
		For an integer matrix \(M\), write
		\[
		N=U^{-1}MU=\begin{pmatrix}A&H\\B&C\end{pmatrix}.
		\]
		Multiplying \(\mu^TM=\mu^T\) on the right by \(U\) gives
		\[
		(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_r,0,\ldots,0)N
		=(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_r,0,\ldots,0).
		\]
		The independence of the \(\gamma_i\) implies that this equality
		holds exactly when \(A=I_r\) and \(H=0\).
		For such a matrix, \(\det M=\det N=\det C\). Hence \(M\) is
		unimodular exactly when \(C\in\operatorname{GL}_s(\mathbb Z)\), with no
		restriction on \(B\).
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{th:isotropy-LFD-An}
		Let \(D_\mu\ne0\) be a locally finite derivation of \(A_n\).
		The automorphisms commuting with \(D_\mu\) are precisely
		\[
		\rho(x_i)=\lambda_i x^{e_i+\ell_i},\qquad
		\lambda_i\in\Bbbk^\ast,\quad \ell_i\in L_\mu,\quad 1\leq i\leq n,
		\]
		for which
		\[
		(e_1+\ell_1\ \cdots\ e_n+\ell_n)\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb Z).
		\]
		Equivalently, fix the matrix \(U\) from
		Proposition~\ref{prop:structure-Gmu}. All such automorphisms, and only
		these, are obtained by choosing arbitrary
		\[
		\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\in\Bbbk^\ast,\qquad
		B\in M_{s\times r}(\mathbb Z),\qquad C\in\operatorname{GL}_s(\mathbb Z),
		\]
		setting
		\[
		M=U\begin{pmatrix}I_r&0\\B&C\end{pmatrix}U^{-1},
		\]
		and defining \(\rho(x_i)=\lambda_i x^{Me_i}\).
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The first description follows from
		Proposition~\ref{isotropy-condition-An}, since
		\(\mu^Tm_i=\mu_i\) is equivalent to \(m_i-e_i\in L_\mu\).
		The parametrization of all admissible matrices is given by
		Proposition~\ref{prop:structure-Gmu}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- coro-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:independent-An}
		If \(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n\) are linearly independent over \(\mathbb Q\),
		then the automorphisms commuting with \(D_\mu\) are precisely
		\[
		\rho(x_i)=\lambda_i x_i,\qquad
		\lambda_i\in\Bbbk^\ast,\quad 1\leq i\leq n.
		\]
<!-- end coro-1 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
In this case \(L_\mu=\{0\}\), so the assertion follows from
		Theorem~\ref{th:isotropy-LFD-An}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- rem-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:group-structure}
		The preceding descriptions also identify the abstract isotropy group.
		Set \(G_\mu=\{M\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb Z):\mu^TM=\mu^T\}\).
		In the adapted basis, multiplication is given by
		\[
		\begin{pmatrix}I_r&0\\B&C\end{pmatrix}
		\begin{pmatrix}I_r&0\\B'&C'\end{pmatrix}
		=\begin{pmatrix}I_r&0\\B+CB'&CC'\end{pmatrix}.
		\]
		Consequently,
		\[
		G_\mu\simeq\mathbb Z^{r(n-r)}\rtimes\operatorname{GL}_{n-r}(\mathbb Z),
		\]
		where \(C\) acts on \(B\) by left multiplication.
		The map \(\rho\mapsto M_\rho\) is a surjective homomorphism from
		\(\operatorname{Aut}_{D_\mu}(A_n)\) to \(G_\mu\), with kernel the diagonal scalings,
		and it splits by \(M\mapsto\sigma_M\), where
		\(\sigma_M(x^\alpha)=x^{M\alpha}\). Thus
		\[
		\operatorname{Aut}_{D_\mu}(A_n)\simeq G_\mu\ltimes(\Bbbk^\ast)^n,
		\]
		with the torus as the normal factor. Explicitly, if
		\(\tau_\lambda(x_i)=\lambda_i x_i\), then
		\[
		\sigma_M\tau_\lambda\sigma_M^{-1}=\tau_{M\cdot\lambda},
		\qquad (M\cdot\lambda)_i=\lambda^{M^{-1}e_i}.
		\]
		For \(n=2\) and \(r=1\), the matrix group is
		\(\mathbb Z\rtimes\{\pm1\}\), where \(-1\) acts by negation;
		this is the infinite dihedral group \(D_\infty\).
		For \(r=n\), the isotropy group is \((\Bbbk^\ast)^n\).
		If \(\mu=0\), every automorphism commutes with \(D_\mu\), and
		\(\operatorname{Aut}_{D_\mu}(A_n)\simeq\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb Z)\ltimes(\Bbbk^\ast)^n\).
<!-- end rem-2 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:flow-isotropy}
		For \(\rho\in\operatorname{Aut}_{\Bbbk}(A_n)\), the following are equivalent:
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item \(\rho D_\mu=D_\mu\rho\);
			\item \(\mu^TM_\rho=\mu^T\);
			\item \(\rho\Phi_t^\ast=\Phi_t^\ast\rho\) for every \(t\in\Bbbk\);
			\item \(F_\rho\circ\Phi_t=\Phi_t\circ F_\rho\) for every \(t\in\Bbbk\).
		\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The equivalence between (1) and (2) follows from
		Proposition~\ref{isotropy-condition-An}.
		We prove that (2) and (3) are equivalent. For each \(i\), write
		\(m_i=(m_{1i},\ldots,m_{ni})^T\). Thus
		\[
		\rho(x_i)=\lambda_i x^{m_i}
		=\lambda_i x_1^{m_{1i}}\cdots x_n^{m_{ni}}.
		\]
		By definition, \(\Phi_t^\ast(f)=f\circ\Phi_t\), so
		$
		\Phi_t^\ast(x_j)=e^{\mu_jt}x_j$, for $j=1,\ldots,n$. Since \(\rho\in\operatorname{Aut}_{\Bbbk}(A_n)\), we have
		\[
		(\rho\circ\Phi_t^\ast)(x_i)
		=\rho(e^{\mu_i t}x_i)
		=e^{\mu_i t}\lambda_i x^{m_i}.
		\]
		On the other hand, \(\Phi_t^\ast\) is a
		\(\Bbbk\)-automorphism, and hence
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			(\Phi_t^\ast\circ\rho)(x_i)
			&=\Phi_t^\ast\left(
			\lambda_i x_1^{m_{1i}}\cdots x_n^{m_{ni}}
			\right)\\
			&=\lambda_i
			\left(e^{\mu_1t}x_1\right)^{m_{1i}}
			\cdots
			\left(e^{\mu_nt}x_n\right)^{m_{ni}}\\
			&=\lambda_i
			e^{(\mu_1m_{1i}+\cdots+\mu_nm_{ni})t}
			x_1^{m_{1i}}\cdots x_n^{m_{ni}}\\
			&=\lambda_i e^{(\mu^Tm_i)t}x^{m_i}.
		\end{aligned}
		\]
		Therefore,
		\[
		\rho\circ\Phi_t^\ast=\Phi_t^\ast\circ\rho
		\quad\text{for every }t\in\Bbbk
		\]
		if and only if
		\[
		e^{\mu_i t}=e^{(\mu^Tm_i)t}
		\quad\text{for every }t\in\Bbbk
		\text{ and every }i.
		\]
		Differentiating these identities at \(t=0\) gives
		\(\mu_i=\mu^Tm_i\) for every \(i\). Conversely, these
		equalities imply the exponential identities above.
		As the \(m_i\) are the columns of \(M_\rho\), this is
		equivalent to
		\[
		\mu^TM_\rho=\mu^T.
		\]
		This proves the equivalence between (2) and (3).
		
		Finally, \(F_\rho^\ast=\rho\), and pullback reverses
		the order of composition. Thus
		\[
		(\Phi_t\circ F_\rho)^\ast
		=\rho\circ\Phi_t^\ast,
		\qquad
		(F_\rho\circ\Phi_t)^\ast
		=\Phi_t^\ast\circ\rho.
		\]
		Since morphisms of affine varieties are determined by
		their pullbacks on coordinate rings, (3) and (4)
		are equivalent.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- prop-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:first-integrals}
		For \(\ell\in\mathbb Z^n\), the Laurent monomial \(x^\ell\) is
		constant along the flow if and only if \(\ell\in L_\mu\). Moreover,
		\[
		A_n^{D_\mu}:=\ker D_\mu
		=\bigoplus_{\ell\in L_\mu}\Bbbk x^\ell.
		\]
		If \(v_1,\ldots,v_s\) is a basis of \(L_\mu\), where \(s=n-r\), then
		\[
		A_n^{D_\mu}
		=\Bbbk[x^{v_1},x^{-v_1},\ldots,x^{v_s},x^{-v_s}]
		\simeq\Bbbk[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_s^{\pm1}].
		\]
		For \(s=0\), this algebra is understood to be \(\Bbbk\).
<!-- end prop-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
We have
		\[
		\Phi_t^\ast(x^\ell)=e^{(\mu^T\ell)t}x^\ell,
		\qquad D_\mu(x^\ell)=(\mu^T\ell)x^\ell.
		\]
		Thus \(x^\ell\) is constant along every trajectory exactly when
		\(\mu^T\ell=0\). The description of the kernel follows because
		Laurent monomials form a basis of eigenvectors for \(D_\mu\).
		Every \(\ell\in L_\mu\) is an integral combination of the \(v_j\),
		which gives the displayed generators. Finally, the map
		\(t_j\mapsto x^{v_j}\) is injective because distinct integer
		combinations of the \(v_j\) give distinct Laurent monomials.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
